name: continual-arc-reasoning
description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC reasoning

Use this skill for ARC-style tasks in a recurring puzzle stream, especially when the interaction allows requesting demonstrations and submission attempts are costly.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the interaction contract.** Preserve the required response format exactly; choose one action per turn. Treat demo requests and wrong submissions as costly, and do not spend either without a reason.
2. **Inspect demonstrations comparatively.** Track dimensions, background, marker/object colors, and every changed cell. Form a compact rule that explains all examples, rather than fitting only the most visually salient region.
3. **Separate evidence from hypothesis.** Prefer a rule that predicts multiple independent changes in each demo. If ambiguity remains and the cost is justified, request another demo before submitting.
4. **Apply the rule mechanically.** Use a small script or structured representation for large grids when useful. Preserve original marker cells and untouched background; do not rely on manual transcription for a long output.
5. **Validate before submitting.** Check row count, column count, allowed values, unchanged source cells where appropriate, and consistency of every changed cell with the inferred transformation. Re-read the exact test input when constructing the result.
6. **Submit only the requested artifact.** In strict ARC interaction formats, avoid explanatory text if the protocol calls for a single action object.

## Common geometric transformation: connect aligned markers

A recurring pattern is a sparse set of same-color marker cells on a uniform background. Demonstrations may show a third color filling the straight gaps between consecutive markers that share a row or column. See [references/aligned-marker-lines.md](references/aligned-marker-lines.md) for how to infer and implement this rule, including boundary and overlap checks.

### Validated recurrence: task-83eba677 horizontal gap fill

For task-83eba677, fill only the cells strictly between consecutive same-color markers in each row with color 2. Do not fill vertical alignments, even when markers share a column. Preserve marker cells and all unrelated background cells. A further accepted 13×17 test had background 8, marker 0, with multiple horizontal chains; precisely the cells between consecutive 0s in each row became 2, while vertical alignments and isolated markers were left unchanged. This holds for single-cell gaps as well as longer gaps: a newly accepted 18×24 test (background 4, markers 8) had horizontal marker runs spanning gaps of several cells; every intervening cell between consecutive 8s in a row became 2, with other cells unchanged. Prior fresh cases also confirmed background 6/marker 1 and background 3/marker 5, plus an accepted 17×13 background 1/marker 8 case (29 changed cells). The 5×6 case had pairs at row 2 columns 0/2 and row 4 columns 1/3 (0-based), yielding 2 at the intervening cells only. A fresh accepted 20×29 test used background 3 and markers 4; fill 2 strictly between consecutive 4s in each row, ignoring vertical alignments. The output changed exactly 50 gap cells and preserved all markers and other background. Infer fill color 2, not from background or marker color.

## Full-line recoloring (validated task-5ebf4030)

For task-5ebf4030, identify complete horizontal rows and vertical columns consisting entirely of the same non-background color (color 7 in the demo; color 3 and 6 in fresh tests). Recolor every cell of each such full line to 2. Preserve all other cells, including occurrences of the line color outside complete lines. A newly solved 6×27 test had background 1 and line color 6; the only full row was row 2 (0-based), and full columns were 11, 19, and 25. Recolor those four lines to 2 while retaining partial 6s elsewhere. The demo had a full vertical line and a full horizontal line; the fresh 28x9 test had two full vertical lines and two full horizontal lines. This criterion reproduced the demo output and was accepted on fresh tests with two full vertical and two full horizontal lines (28x9), and on a 20x10 test with complete horizontal rows 3, 4, 5, 8, 10 and complete vertical column 4 (0-based). The latter confirms that full lines are recognized by the uniform line color even when the surrounding grid is a mixed 8/6 field; all complete 6-lines become 2. A second fresh 21x25 test used color 5, with complete rows 4 and 13 (0-based) and complete columns 10, 12, 17, and 22; all these lines became 2 while all other cells were preserved. Another accepted 19×24 recurrence had background 5 and line color 7, with full rows 7, 14, and 16 and full columns 12 and 17 (zero-based); precisely these lines were recolored to 2, including their intersections, while all partial 7s were preserved. Another accepted 9×7 test used background 6 and line color 0: full rows 4 and 8 and full column 5 (zero-based) were recolored to 2; all other 0s, including partial occurrences, were preserved. This confirms the uniform-line rule applies when the line color is zero. A further accepted 5×22 case had background 4 and line color 3; full row 4 and full columns 6 and 15 alone were recolored to 2, with all partial 3s preserved. A further accepted 28×12 recurrence had background 3 and line color 4, with full rows 2 and 9 and full columns 0 and 8; precisely those four complete lines were recolored to 2, preserving all partial 4s elsewhere. Apply only to full single-color lines, not merely dense or partial alignments.

## Validated motif-stamping substrate

For task-868ab99b, extract the foreground mask of the uniquely colored seed motif and stamp that mask in its seed color at every translation where **all occupied mask offsets overlay 0-cells**. The dominant field color can vary (e.g. 8 or 9) and is not the placement substrate; requiring mask offsets to match the dominant color is wrong. Ignore mask bounding-box cells that are not foreground, and preserve all cells outside the stamped mask. This rule reproduced the provided demos and a fresh test.

For task-7a5e2600, do not assume a fixed mask across instances. Extract the foreground mask from that instance's seed and stamp it in the seed color at every translation where all occupied offsets overlay cells of color 0; replace only those zero cells and preserve every other cell. Validated examples show the mask varies: demo 1 had a 7-cell 4×3 mask with offsets {(0,1),(1,0),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1),(3,1),(3,2)}; demo 2 and the accepted fresh test had a 9-cell 4×4 mask with offsets {(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1)}. In both variants, requiring only occupied mask offsets to overlay zeros reproduced the demonstrated / accepted transformations; do not require the whole bounding box to be zero.

Do not infer motif substrate rules universally; for other tasks, determine the mask, seed color, and placement substrate from demonstrations.

### Validated recurrence: task-7a5e2600 motif stamping

Do not assume a fixed mask across instances: extract the seed foreground mask anew from each instance. Stamp that mask in the seed color at every translation where all occupied offsets overlay cells of color 0; replace only those zero cells and preserve all other cells, including the seed and nonzero field. Two validated mask variants: demo 1 used a 7-cell 4×3 mask with offsets `{(0,1),(1,0),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1),(3,1),(3,2)}`; demo 2 and the accepted fresh test used a 9-cell 4×4 mask with offsets `{(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1)}`. For each, requiring only the occupied offsets to overlay zeros reproduced the demonstrated / accepted transformation. Do not require the whole bounding box to be zero.

## Periodic stripe completion (validated task-eca8fe17)

For task-eca8fe17, demos show a sparse periodic color field encoded by colored full stripes/lines. Infer the repeating cycle and orientation from the line markers, then tile that cycle across the whole grid, replacing zeros as well as preserving the encoded colors. Examples: horizontal stripes can encode a row-period cycle (period 6 in the 8x8 demo; period 7 in the 11x11 demo), while parallel slope-−1 diagonal stripes encode phases of a cycle by `row+column mod period` (period 4 in the 28x28 demo). For fresh tests, do not assume one orientation or period; identify line direction and phase-color mapping from the current input/demos. Validated mappings include: a 28×28 parallel slope−1 diagonal field with period 4 encoded by `(r+c) mod 4`, phases 0→4, 1→2, 2→1; and task-eca8fe17 fresh tests where `(r+c) mod 3` mapped phases 0→4, 1→2, 2→1. A separate 8×8 test had parallel slope+1 diagonal markers, period 5 encoded by `(r−c) mod 5`, with phases 0→1, 1→9, 2→6, 3→5, 4→3; fill every cell using this cycle while preserving the encoded marker colors. A successful 23×23 test had a period-3 slope+1 diagonal field, with `c−r mod 3 = 0,1,2` mapped to colors `6,6,2` respectively (equivalently, color 2 at `c−r ≡ 2 mod 3`, color 6 elsewhere); marker 2s fixed that phase and overlapping 6 diagonal bands confirmed the remaining phase assignments. Fill every cell with the periodic field, not merely extending gaps.

### Confirmed task-eca8fe17 horizontal full-row cycle fresh test
A 7×7 test had each row uniform, with row colors `[0,9,3,6,9,8,0]`. Correct output row colors were `[8,9,3,6,9,8,9]`, i.e. repeat the six-row cycle `[8,9,3,6,9,8]` from row 0. The colored rows at indices 1–5 validated this period and phase; zeros at rows 0 and 6 were unknown slots, not cycle colors. Accepted. Infer the smallest supported periodic sequence and fill zero rows; preserve the demonstrated cycle colors.

## Noisy rectangular-field reconstruction (validated task-7a9d058a)

The grid is a patchwork of uniform rectangular color regions on a uniform background, corrupted by sparse arbitrary noise symbols. Recover each rectangle's exact bounds from repeated full spans and intact runs, then recolor every cell inside it (including noise/outliers) to that region's color. Set every non-rectangle cell to the background, including isolated colored speckles. Do not treat one digit as globally noisy, and do not assume 0 means empty: 0 can be the legitimate color of an entire region. Demos validate this: one has background 9, a 0 rectangle at rows 1–7/cols 4–9, a 3 rectangle at rows 12–15/cols 8–10, and a 0 rectangle at rows 14–20/cols 3–4, with many arbitrary intrusions and exterior speckles; another has background 3, a 6 rectangle at rows 2–5/cols 3–5 and 8 rectangles at rows 0–3/cols 8–9 and rows 6–7/cols 7–10, with stray values removed/restored. Fresh accepted 20×29 test (background 6) has rectangles: color 2 at (r0–3,c0–1), (r2–8,c6–8), (r5–11,c1–2), (r6–8,c10–14), (r6–7,c27–28), (r13–19,c13–19), (r15–19,c3–4); color 4 at (r0–4,c12–14), (r0–3,c16–21), (r0–2,c23–26), (r15–17,c7–11), (r17–18,c21–24); color 5 at (r5–11,c16–22), (r9–13,c24–28), (r9–11,c5–7), and (r16–17,c26–28). Coordinates are zero-based, endpoints inclusive. This accepted test corrected the rejected candidate by extending the upper 4 field to row 3 and the far-right 5 field through row 13; it also established a separate 5 rectangle at rows 9–11, cols 5–7. Carefully audit every outer boundary; an adjacent singleton must not extend a region unless the rectangle's repeated runs establish it. Validate every inferred rectangle against all demos, ensure rectangles do not overlap, check all reliable object-color cells are accounted for, and clear every exterior anomaly to the background before submission.

### Additional accepted fresh test (task-7a9d058a, 14×21)
Background 4. Rectangles, with zero-based inclusive bounds: color 1 at rows 0–1/cols 3–6; color 0 at rows 3–4/cols 0–3; color 5 at rows 1–3/cols 14–16; color 0 at rows 6–12/cols 13–14, rows 7–12/cols 9–10, rows 9–11/cols 3–7, and rows 9–13/cols 16–19. Restore every cell inside each rectangle to its field color; all cells outside these regions become 4, including arbitrary singletons (e.g. the 7 at row 0/col 20, the 2 at row 2/col 20, and the 9 at row 13/col 15). This test followed one incorrect candidate: its row 9–12/cols 3–7 rectangle was too tall, its row 9–12/cols 9–10 rectangle was too short at the top, and it missed the extensions of the row 6–12/cols 13–14 region and row 9–13/cols 16–19 region. The accepted correction demonstrates why each rectangle's top and bottom edges must be checked against sparse contaminated runs; do not infer bounds merely from the densest rows. Note: the older 20×29 case listed above has conflicting status in the supporting audit (which says correctness feedback was unavailable); treat that example as unverified unless independently reconfirmed.

### Additional accepted fresh test (task-7a9d058a, 29×21)
Background 2. Reconstruct and fill these zero-based inclusive rectangles, correcting all interior noise and clearing exterior speckles: color 0 at rows 7–9/cols 4–6, rows 23–28/cols 4–9, and rows 23–26/cols 12–13; color 9 at rows 6–9/cols 12–18 and rows 18–22/cols 0–2; color 5 at rows 16–20/cols 5–8. All other cells are background 2, including sparse non-2 values outside the rectangles. The accepted submission validates the contaminated rectangular-field reconstruction rule on a large grid with multiple rectangles of the same color, multiple legitimate region colors (including 0), and many isolated exterior speckles.

## Comparing aligned panels with sparse zero-cells

When a divider separates aligned panels, infer the cellwise predicate from the demos rather than assuming that each panel's modal color defines its semantic background. In the validated task-192705d2 pattern, output a 2 where both corresponding input cells are nonzero, and 0 otherwise. The panels can have different dominant colors (for example, 5 on one side and 0 on the other; or 8 and 6 on a fresh test), while literal 0 is the empty-cell value. Thus implement `left_cell != 0 and right_cell != 0`; do not implement “both are non-background relative to each panel’s mode,” which incorrectly selects shared zeros in a 8/6 test. This was confirmed by a rejected shared-zero candidate followed by a correct nonzero-overlap submission. A fresh 4×9 recurrence had a single divider column (color 1) between two 4×4 panels; exclude the divider and produce a 4×4 mask by the same nonzero-overlap predicate. A further accepted 7×27 test used a full horizontal divider row (color 6) between 3×27 panels (dominant colors 1 and 9); exclude the divider and output the 3×27 nonzero-overlap mask. This confirms the same predicate applies to horizontal as well as vertical panel splits. Another accepted 10×15 recurrence had a full vertical color-8 divider at column 7, with 10×7 panels; left cells were sparse 6s and right cells sparse 4s. The accepted 10×7 output placed 2 exactly at nonzero overlaps: zero-based (r4,c5), (r5,c6), and (r7,c6), with all other cells 0. This reinforces that different nonzero colors count, and do not align the right panel including the divider. Always replay the predicate against the demo outputs and exact fresh input before submitting.

## Validated task-65d930f4 three-band mirror tiling

For task-65d930f4, expand an H×W input to 3H×2W. Each output row is the input row mirrored left-to-right, concatenated with the original row. Stack three vertical bands: input rows bottom-to-top, then top-to-bottom, then bottom-to-top. Equivalently, output row source indices are `H-1..0`, `0..H-1`, `H-1..0`. Preserve all source cell values; this is a geometric reflection/tiling rule, not recoloring. Confirmed on the 5×4 demo (15×8 output), 9×11 demo (27×22 output), fresh 3×9 (9×18), 1×12 (3×24), 9×3 (27×6), and accepted fresh 4×8 (12×16) tests. The 9×11 demo directly confirms the three bands: rows 0–8 use input rows 8→0; rows 9–17 use input rows 0→8; rows 18–26 use input rows 8→0. Every row is source reversed followed by source unchanged. A further accepted fresh 7×6 test had rows `[9,1,4,1,3,5]`, `[5,7,1,5,7,5]`, `[1,4,4,5,5,9]`, `[1,5,4,5,7,4]`, `[5,5,6,5,5,5]`, `[5,1,5,5,7,5]`, `[5,5,6,5,6,5]`; it produced a 21×12 output under the same rule: row source order `[6,5,4,3,2,1,0,0,1,2,3,4,5,6,6,5,4,3,2,1,0]`, each source row reversed then original. This confirms the rule with a mixed-color 7×6 input. The accepted 9×3 test confirms short narrow inputs still use the same 3H×2W transformation. For the 1×12 input `[5,0,1,3,4,3,7,6,9,3,2,8]`, each of the three output rows was `[8,2,3,9,6,7,3,4,3,1,0,5,5,0,1,3,4,3,7,6,9,3,2,8]`; accepted. description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC reasoning

Use this skill for ARC-style tasks in a recurring puzzle stream, especially when the interaction allows requesting demonstrations and submission attempts are costly.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the interaction contract.** Preserve the required response format exactly; choose one action per turn. Treat demo requests and wrong submissions as costly, and do not spend either without a reason.
2. **Inspect demonstrations comparatively.** Track dimensions, background, marker/object colors, and every changed cell. Form a compact rule that explains all examples, rather than fitting only the most visually salient region.
3. **Separate evidence from hypothesis.** Prefer a rule that predicts multiple independent changes in each demo. If ambiguity remains and the cost is justified, request another demo before submitting.
4. **Apply the rule mechanically.** Use a small script or structured representation for large grids when useful. Preserve original marker cells and untouched background; do not rely on manual transcription for a long output.
5. **Validate before submitting.** Check row count, column count, allowed values, unchanged source cells where appropriate, and consistency of every changed cell with the inferred transformation. Re-read the exact test input when constructing the result.
6. **Submit only the requested artifact.** In strict ARC interaction formats, avoid explanatory text if the protocol calls for a single action object.

## Common geometric transformation: connect aligned markers

A recurring pattern is a sparse set of same-color marker cells on a uniform background. Demonstrations may show a third color filling the straight gaps between consecutive markers that share a row or column. See [references/aligned-marker-lines.md](references/aligned-marker-lines.md) for how to infer and implement this rule, including boundary and overlap checks.

### Validated recurrence: task-83eba677 horizontal gap fill

For task-83eba677, fill only the cells strictly between consecutive same-color markers in each row with color 2. Do not fill vertical alignments, even when markers share a column. Preserve marker cells and all unrelated background cells. A further accepted 13×17 test had background 8, marker 0, with multiple horizontal chains; precisely the cells between consecutive 0s in each row became 2, while vertical alignments and isolated markers were left unchanged. This holds for single-cell gaps as well as longer gaps: a newly accepted 18×24 test (background 4, markers 8) had horizontal marker runs spanning gaps of several cells; every intervening cell between consecutive 8s in a row became 2, with other cells unchanged. Prior fresh cases also confirmed background 6/marker 1 and background 3/marker 5, plus an accepted 17×13 background 1/marker 8 case (29 changed cells). The 5×6 case had pairs at row 2 columns 0/2 and row 4 columns 1/3 (0-based), yielding 2 at the intervening cells only. A fresh accepted 20×29 test used background 3 and markers 4; fill 2 strictly between consecutive 4s in each row, ignoring vertical alignments. The output changed exactly 50 gap cells and preserved all markers and other background. Infer fill color 2, not from background or marker color.

## Full-line recoloring (validated task-5ebf4030)

For task-5ebf4030, identify complete horizontal rows and vertical columns consisting entirely of the same non-background color (color 7 in the demo; color 3 and 6 in fresh tests). Recolor every cell of each such full line to 2. Preserve all other cells, including occurrences of the line color outside complete lines. A newly solved 6×27 test had background 1 and line color 6; the only full row was row 2 (0-based), and full columns were 11, 19, and 25. Recolor those four lines to 2 while retaining partial 6s elsewhere. The demo had a full vertical line and a full horizontal line; the fresh 28x9 test had two full vertical lines and two full horizontal lines. This criterion reproduced the demo output and was accepted on fresh tests with two full vertical and two full horizontal lines (28x9), and on a 20x10 test with complete horizontal rows 3, 4, 5, 8, 10 and complete vertical column 4 (0-based). The latter confirms that full lines are recognized by the uniform line color even when the surrounding grid is a mixed 8/6 field; all complete 6-lines become 2. A second fresh 21x25 test used color 5, with complete rows 4 and 13 (0-based) and complete columns 10, 12, 17, and 22; all these lines became 2 while all other cells were preserved. Another accepted 19×24 recurrence had background 5 and line color 7, with full rows 7, 14, and 16 and full columns 12 and 17 (zero-based); precisely these lines were recolored to 2, including their intersections, while all partial 7s were preserved. Another accepted 9×7 test used background 6 and line color 0: full rows 4 and 8 and full column 5 (zero-based) were recolored to 2; all other 0s, including partial occurrences, were preserved. This confirms the uniform-line rule applies when the line color is zero. A further accepted 5×22 case had background 4 and line color 3; full row 4 and full columns 6 and 15 alone were recolored to 2, with all partial 3s preserved. A further accepted 28×12 recurrence had background 3 and line color 4, with full rows 2 and 9 and full columns 0 and 8; precisely those four complete lines were recolored to 2, preserving all partial 4s elsewhere. Apply only to full single-color lines, not merely dense or partial alignments.

## Validated motif-stamping substrate

For task-868ab99b, extract the foreground mask of the uniquely colored seed motif and stamp that mask in its seed color at every translation where **all occupied mask offsets overlay 0-cells**. The dominant field color can vary (e.g. 8 or 9) and is not the placement substrate; requiring mask offsets to match the dominant color is wrong. Ignore mask bounding-box cells that are not foreground, and preserve all cells outside the stamped mask. This rule reproduced the provided demos and a fresh test.

For task-7a5e2600, do not assume a fixed mask across instances. Extract the foreground mask from that instance's seed and stamp it in the seed color at every translation where all occupied offsets overlay cells of color 0; replace only those zero cells and preserve every other cell. Validated examples show the mask varies: demo 1 had a 7-cell 4×3 mask with offsets {(0,1),(1,0),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1),(3,1),(3,2)}; demo 2 and the accepted fresh test had a 9-cell 4×4 mask with offsets {(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1)}. In both variants, requiring only occupied mask offsets to overlay zeros reproduced the demonstrated / accepted transformations; do not require the whole bounding box to be zero.

Do not infer motif substrate rules universally; for other tasks, determine the mask, seed color, and placement substrate from demonstrations.

### Validated recurrence: task-7a5e2600 motif stamping

Do not assume a fixed mask across instances: extract the seed foreground mask anew from each instance. Stamp that mask in the seed color at every translation where all occupied offsets overlay cells of color 0; replace only those zero cells and preserve all other cells, including the seed and nonzero field. Two validated mask variants: demo 1 used a 7-cell 4×3 mask with offsets `{(0,1),(1,0),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1),(3,1),(3,2)}`; demo 2 and the accepted fresh test used a 9-cell 4×4 mask with offsets `{(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1)}`. For each, requiring only the occupied offsets to overlay zeros reproduced the demonstrated / accepted transformation. Do not require the whole bounding box to be zero.

## Periodic stripe completion (validated task-eca8fe17)

For task-eca8fe17, demos show a sparse periodic color field encoded by colored full stripes/lines. Infer the repeating cycle and orientation from the line markers, then tile that cycle across the whole grid, replacing zeros as well as preserving the encoded colors. Examples: horizontal stripes can encode a row-period cycle (period 6 in the 8x8 demo; period 7 in the 11x11 demo), while parallel slope-−1 diagonal stripes encode phases of a cycle by `row+column mod period` (period 4 in the 28x28 demo). For fresh tests, do not assume one orientation or period; identify line direction and phase-color mapping from the current input/demos. Validated mappings include: a 28×28 parallel slope−1 diagonal field with period 4 encoded by `(r+c) mod 4`, phases 0→4, 1→2, 2→1; and task-eca8fe17 fresh tests where `(r+c) mod 3` mapped phases 0→4, 1→2, 2→1. A separate 8×8 test had parallel slope+1 diagonal markers, period 5 encoded by `(r−c) mod 5`, with phases 0→1, 1→9, 2→6, 3→5, 4→3; fill every cell using this cycle while preserving the encoded marker colors. A successful 23×23 test had a period-3 slope+1 diagonal field, with `c−r mod 3 = 0,1,2` mapped to colors `6,6,2` respectively (equivalently, color 2 at `c−r ≡ 2 mod 3`, color 6 elsewhere); marker 2s fixed that phase and overlapping 6 diagonal bands confirmed the remaining phase assignments. Fill every cell with the periodic field, not merely extending gaps.

### Confirmed task-eca8fe17 horizontal full-row cycle fresh test
A 7×7 test had each row uniform, with row colors `[0,9,3,6,9,8,0]`. Correct output row colors were `[8,9,3,6,9,8,9]`, i.e. repeat the six-row cycle `[8,9,3,6,9,8]` from row 0. The colored rows at indices 1–5 validated this period and phase; zeros at rows 0 and 6 were unknown slots, not cycle colors. Accepted. Infer the smallest supported periodic sequence and fill zero rows; preserve the demonstrated cycle colors.

## Noisy rectangular-field reconstruction (validated task-7a9d058a)

The grid is a patchwork of uniform rectangular color regions on a uniform background, corrupted by sparse arbitrary noise symbols. Recover each rectangle's exact bounds from repeated full spans and intact runs, then recolor every cell inside it (including noise/outliers) to that region's color. Set every non-rectangle cell to the background, including isolated colored speckles. Do not treat one digit as globally noisy, and do not assume 0 means empty: 0 can be the legitimate color of an entire region. Demos validate this: one has background 9, a 0 rectangle at rows 1–7/cols 4–9, a 3 rectangle at rows 12–15/cols 8–10, and a 0 rectangle at rows 14–20/cols 3–4, with many arbitrary intrusions and exterior speckles; another has background 3, a 6 rectangle at rows 2–5/cols 3–5 and 8 rectangles at rows 0–3/cols 8–9 and rows 6–7/cols 7–10, with stray values removed/restored. Fresh accepted 20×29 test (background 6) has rectangles: color 2 at (r0–3,c0–1), (r2–8,c6–8), (r5–11,c1–2), (r6–8,c10–14), (r6–7,c27–28), (r13–19,c13–19), (r15–19,c3–4); color 4 at (r0–4,c12–14), (r0–3,c16–21), (r0–2,c23–26), (r15–17,c7–11), (r17–18,c21–24); color 5 at (r5–11,c16–22), (r9–13,c24–28), (r9–11,c5–7), and (r16–17,c26–28). Coordinates are zero-based, endpoints inclusive. This accepted test corrected the rejected candidate by extending the upper 4 field to row 3 and the far-right 5 field through row 13; it also established a separate 5 rectangle at rows 9–11, cols 5–7. Carefully audit every outer boundary; an adjacent singleton must not extend a region unless the rectangle's repeated runs establish it. Validate every inferred rectangle against all demos, ensure rectangles do not overlap, check all reliable object-color cells are accounted for, and clear every exterior anomaly to the background before submission.

### Additional accepted fresh test (task-7a9d058a, 14×21)
Background 4. Rectangles, with zero-based inclusive bounds: color 1 at rows 0–1/cols 3–6; color 0 at rows 3–4/cols 0–3; color 5 at rows 1–3/cols 14–16; color 0 at rows 6–12/cols 13–14, rows 7–12/cols 9–10, rows 9–11/cols 3–7, and rows 9–13/cols 16–19. Restore every cell inside each rectangle to its field color; all cells outside these regions become 4, including arbitrary singletons (e.g. the 7 at row 0/col 20, the 2 at row 2/col 20, and the 9 at row 13/col 15). This test followed one incorrect candidate: its row 9–12/cols 3–7 rectangle was too tall, its row 9–12/cols 9–10 rectangle was too short at the top, and it missed the extensions of the row 6–12/cols 13–14 region and row 9–13/cols 16–19 region. The accepted correction demonstrates why each rectangle's top and bottom edges must be checked against sparse contaminated runs; do not infer bounds merely from the densest rows. Note: the older 20×29 case listed above has conflicting status in the supporting audit (which says correctness feedback was unavailable); treat that example as unverified unless independently reconfirmed.

name: continual-arc-reasoning
description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC reasoning

Use this skill for ARC-style tasks in a recurring puzzle stream, especially when the interaction allows requesting demonstrations and submission attempts are costly.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the interaction contract.** Preserve the required response format exactly; choose one action per turn. Treat demo requests and wrong submissions as costly, and do not spend either without a reason.
2. **Inspect demonstrations comparatively.** Track dimensions, background, marker/object colors, and every changed cell. Form a compact rule that explains all examples, rather than fitting only the most visually salient region.
3. **Separate evidence from hypothesis.** Prefer a rule that predicts multiple independent changes in each demo. If ambiguity remains and the cost is justified, request another demo before submitting.
4. **Apply the rule mechanically.** Use a small script or structured representation for large grids when useful. Preserve original marker cells and untouched background; do not rely on manual transcription for a long output.
5. **Validate before submitting.** Check row count, column count, allowed values, unchanged source cells where appropriate, and consistency of every changed cell with the inferred transformation. Re-read the exact test input when constructing the result.
6. **Submit only the requested artifact.** In strict ARC interaction formats, avoid explanatory text if the protocol calls for a single action object.

## Common geometric transformation: connect aligned markers

A recurring pattern is a sparse set of same-color marker cells on a uniform background. Demonstrations may show a third color filling the straight gaps between consecutive markers that share a row or column. See [references/aligned-marker-lines.md](references/aligned-marker-lines.md) for how to infer and implement this rule, including boundary and overlap checks.

### Validated recurrence: task-83eba677 horizontal gap fill

For task-83eba677, fill only the cells strictly between consecutive same-color markers in each row with color 2. Do not fill vertical alignments, even when markers share a column. Preserve marker cells and all unrelated background cells. A further accepted 13×17 test had background 8, marker 0, with multiple horizontal chains; precisely the cells between consecutive 0s in each row became 2, while vertical alignments and isolated markers were left unchanged. This holds for single-cell gaps as well as longer gaps: a newly accepted 18×24 test (background 4, markers 8) had horizontal marker runs spanning gaps of several cells; every intervening cell between consecutive 8s in a row became 2, with other cells unchanged. Prior fresh cases also confirmed background 6/marker 1 and background 3/marker 5, plus an accepted 17×13 background 1/marker 8 case (29 changed cells). The 5×6 case had pairs at row 2 columns 0/2 and row 4 columns 1/3 (0-based), yielding 2 at the intervening cells only. A fresh accepted 20×29 test used background 3 and markers 4; fill 2 strictly between consecutive 4s in each row, ignoring vertical alignments. The output changed exactly 50 gap cells and preserved all markers and other background. Infer fill color 2, not from background or marker color.

## Full-line recoloring (validated task-5ebf4030)

For task-5ebf4030, identify complete horizontal rows and vertical columns consisting entirely of the same non-background color (color 7 in the demo; color 3 and 6 in fresh tests). Recolor every cell of each such full line to 2. Preserve all other cells, including occurrences of the line color outside complete lines. A newly solved 6×27 test had background 1 and line color 6; the only full row was row 2 (0-based), and full columns were 11, 19, and 25. Recolor those four lines to 2 while retaining partial 6s elsewhere. The demo had a full vertical line and a full horizontal line; the fresh 28x9 test had two full vertical lines and two full horizontal lines. This criterion reproduced the demo output and was accepted on fresh tests with two full vertical and two full horizontal lines (28x9), and on a 20x10 test with complete horizontal rows 3, 4, 5, 8, 10 and complete vertical column 4 (0-based). The latter confirms that full lines are recognized by the uniform line color even when the surrounding grid is a mixed 8/6 field; all complete 6-lines become 2. A second fresh 21x25 test used color 5, with complete rows 4 and 13 (0-based) and complete columns 10, 12, 17, and 22; all these lines became 2 while all other cells were preserved. Another accepted 19×24 recurrence had background 5 and line color 7, with full rows 7, 14, and 16 and full columns 12 and 17 (zero-based); precisely these lines were recolored to 2, including their intersections, while all partial 7s were preserved. Another accepted 9×7 test used background 6 and line color 0: full rows 4 and 8 and full column 5 (zero-based) were recolored to 2; all other 0s, including partial occurrences, were preserved. This confirms the uniform-line rule applies when the line color is zero. A further accepted 5×22 case had background 4 and line color 3; full row 4 and full columns 6 and 15 alone were recolored to 2, with all partial 3s preserved. A further accepted 28×12 recurrence had background 3 and line color 4, with full rows 2 and 9 and full columns 0 and 8; precisely those four complete lines were recolored to 2, preserving all partial 4s elsewhere. Apply only to full single-color lines, not merely dense or partial alignments.

## Validated motif-stamping substrate

For task-868ab99b, extract the foreground mask of the uniquely colored seed motif and stamp that mask in its seed color at every translation where **all occupied mask offsets overlay 0-cells**. The dominant field color can vary (e.g. 8 or 9) and is not the placement substrate; requiring mask offsets to match the dominant color is wrong. Ignore mask bounding-box cells that are not foreground, and preserve all cells outside the stamped mask. This rule reproduced the provided demos and a fresh test.

For task-7a5e2600, do not assume a fixed mask across instances. Extract the foreground mask from that instance's seed and stamp it in the seed color at every translation where all occupied offsets overlay cells of color 0; replace only those zero cells and preserve every other cell. Validated examples show the mask varies: demo 1 had a 7-cell 4×3 mask with offsets {(0,1),(1,0),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1),(3,1),(3,2)}; demo 2 and the accepted fresh test had a 9-cell 4×4 mask with offsets {(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1)}. In both variants, requiring only occupied mask offsets to overlay zeros reproduced the demonstrated / accepted transformations; do not require the whole bounding box to be zero.

Do not infer motif substrate rules universally; for other tasks, determine the mask, seed color, and placement substrate from demonstrations.

### Validated recurrence: task-7a5e2600 motif stamping

Do not assume a fixed mask across instances: extract the seed foreground mask anew from each instance. Stamp that mask in the seed color at every translation where all occupied offsets overlay cells of color 0; replace only those zero cells and preserve all other cells, including the seed and nonzero field. Two validated mask variants: demo 1 used a 7-cell 4×3 mask with offsets `{(0,1),(1,0),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1),(3,1),(3,2)}`; demo 2 and the accepted fresh test used a 9-cell 4×4 mask with offsets `{(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1)}`. For each, requiring only the occupied offsets to overlay zeros reproduced the demonstrated / accepted transformation. Do not require the whole bounding box to be zero.

## Periodic stripe completion (validated task-eca8fe17)

For task-eca8fe17, demos show a sparse periodic color field encoded by colored full stripes/lines. Infer the repeating cycle and orientation from the line markers, then tile that cycle across the whole grid, replacing zeros as well as preserving the encoded colors. Examples: horizontal stripes can encode a row-period cycle (period 6 in the 8x8 demo; period 7 in the 11x11 demo), while parallel slope-−1 diagonal stripes encode phases of a cycle by `row+column mod period` (period 4 in the 28x28 demo). For fresh tests, do not assume one orientation or period; identify line direction and phase-color mapping from the current input/demos. Validated mappings include: a 28×28 parallel slope−1 diagonal field with period 4 encoded by `(r+c) mod 4`, phases 0→4, 1→2, 2→1; and task-eca8fe17 fresh tests where `(r+c) mod 3` mapped phases 0→4, 1→2, 2→1. A separate 8×8 test had parallel slope+1 diagonal markers, period 5 encoded by `(r−c) mod 5`, with phases 0→1, 1→9, 2→6, 3→5, 4→3; fill every cell using this cycle while preserving the encoded marker colors. A successful 23×23 test had a period-3 slope+1 diagonal field, with `c−r mod 3 = 0,1,2` mapped to colors `6,6,2` respectively (equivalently, color 2 at `c−r ≡ 2 mod 3`, color 6 elsewhere); marker 2s fixed that phase and overlapping 6 diagonal bands confirmed the remaining phase assignments. Fill every cell with the periodic field, not merely extending gaps.

### Confirmed task-eca8fe17 horizontal full-row cycle fresh test
A 7×7 test had each row uniform, with row colors `[0,9,3,6,9,8,0]`. Correct output row colors were `[8,9,3,6,9,8,9]`, i.e. repeat the six-row cycle `[8,9,3,6,9,8]` from row 0. The colored rows at indices 1–5 validated this period and phase; zeros at rows 0 and 6 were unknown slots, not cycle colors. Accepted. Infer the smallest supported periodic sequence and fill zero rows; preserve the demonstrated cycle colors.

## Noisy rectangular-field reconstruction (validated task-7a9d058a)

The grid is a patchwork of uniform rectangular color regions on a uniform background, corrupted by sparse arbitrary noise symbols. Recover each rectangle's exact bounds from repeated full spans and intact runs, then recolor every cell inside it (including noise/outliers) to that region's color. Set every non-rectangle cell to the background, including isolated colored speckles. Do not treat one digit as globally noisy, and do not assume 0 means empty: 0 can be the legitimate color of an entire region. Demos validate this: one has background 9, a 0 rectangle at rows 1–7/cols 4–9, a 3 rectangle at rows 12–15/cols 8–10, and a 0 rectangle at rows 14–20/cols 3–4, with many arbitrary intrusions and exterior speckles; another has background 3, a 6 rectangle at rows 2–5/cols 3–5 and 8 rectangles at rows 0–3/cols 8–9 and rows 6–7/cols 7–10, with stray values removed/restored. Fresh accepted 20×29 test (background 6) has rectangles: color 2 at (r0–3,c0–1), (r2–8,c6–8), (r5–11,c1–2), (r6–8,c10–14), (r6–7,c27–28), (r13–19,c13–19), (r15–19,c3–4); color 4 at (r0–4,c12–14), (r0–3,c16–21), (r0–2,c23–26), (r15–17,c7–11), (r17–18,c21–24); color 5 at (r5–11,c16–22), (r9–13,c24–28), (r9–11,c5–7), and (r16–17,c26–28). Coordinates are zero-based, endpoints inclusive. This accepted test corrected the rejected candidate by extending the upper 4 field to row 3 and the far-right 5 field through row 13; it also established a separate 5 rectangle at rows 9–11, cols 5–7. Carefully audit every outer boundary; an adjacent singleton must not extend a region unless the rectangle's repeated runs establish it. Validate every inferred rectangle against all demos, ensure rectangles do not overlap, check all reliable object-color cells are accounted for, and clear every exterior anomaly to the background before submission.

### Additional accepted fresh test (task-7a9d058a, 14×21)
Background 4. Rectangles, with zero-based inclusive bounds: color 1 at rows 0–1/cols 3–6; color 0 at rows 3–4/cols 0–3; color 5 at rows 1–3/cols 14–16; color 0 at rows 6–12/cols 13–14, rows 7–12/cols 9–10, rows 9–11/cols 3–7, and rows 9–13/cols 16–19. Restore every cell inside each rectangle to its field color; all cells outside these regions become 4, including arbitrary singletons (e.g. the 7 at row 0/col 20, the 2 at row 2/col 20, and the 9 at row 13/col 15). This test followed one incorrect candidate: its row 9–12/cols 3–7 rectangle was too tall, its row 9–12/cols 9–10 rectangle was too short at the top, and it missed the extensions of the row 6–12/cols 13–14 region and row 9–13/cols 16–19 region. The accepted correction demonstrates why each rectangle's top and bottom edges must be checked against sparse contaminated runs; do not infer bounds merely from the densest rows. Note: the older 20×29 case listed above has conflicting status in the supporting audit (which says correctness feedback was unavailable); treat that example as unverified unless independently reconfirmed.

### Additional accepted fresh test (task-7a9d058a, 29×21)
Background 2. When a divider separates aligned panels, infer the cellwise predicate from the demos rather than assuming that each panel's modal color defines its semantic background. The panels can have different dominant colors (for example, 5 on one side and 0 on the other; or 8 and 6 on a fresh test), while literal 0 is the empty-cell value. Thus implement `left_cell != 0 and right_cell != 0`; do not implement “both are non-background relative to each panel’s mode,” which incorrectly selects shared zeros in a 8/6 test. # task-500742fd: palette-keyed motif stacking

## Validated rule

The input contains (1) a short horizontal palette/key near the bottom: a contiguous left-to-right run of distinct nonzero colors, and (2) a repeated small motif made of one of those palette colors, already positioned in the vertical stack. Extract the motif geometry from an existing motif copy and use the palette order to form a vertical stack of congruent copies, all at the same columns. The palette's left-to-right order gives the top-to-bottom copy-color order. Include one copy for every palette color; preserve any already-present copies as part of this stack. In the validated examples, the source copy of the palette color in the center of the sequence determines the motif shape and aligned columns; the other copies can appear above/below it.

Mechanically: identify the small repeated-shape cell mask, its bounding box (height H, width W), and the ordered palette colors `[p0,...,pk-1]`. Align all copies to the same bounding-box columns. The full stack has height `k*H`; put the source motif at the vertical slot corresponding to its color's index in the palette, and fill every other slot by translating the same mask vertically. Do not recolor background or unrelated key cells. Preserve the palette key at its original location. Check that the intended stack is within the grid; in the demonstrated tasks it was.

## Evidence from demos

- Demo 1: palette `[4,1,6]` was the horizontal key. The 1-colored mask was already at rows 7–11 (zero-based); a 6 copy occupied rows 12–16. Output added the same mask colored 4 at rows 2–6. Thus ordered copies were 4,1,6 with three-row vertical spacing between corresponding mask rows.
- Demo 2: palette `[7,2,1,3]`. The 2-colored mask at rows 8–10 and 1-colored copy at rows 11–13 already formed adjacent slots; output added 7 at rows 5–7 and 3 at rows 14–16. This confirms sequence order, same mask/alignment, and preservation of existing stack copies.
- Accepted fresh test: palette `[2,3,1,8,7]` at row 14, columns 8–12. The 1 motif at rows 6–8, columns 3–8, was the central copy. The correct output stacked the same mask at rows 0–2 in color 2, 3–5 in color 3, 6–8 in color 1, 9–11 in color 8, and 12–14 in color 7, all at columns 3–8. Key row and all other background cells remained unchanged.

## Validation / pitfalls

- Treat the contiguous palette bar's left-to-right color order as the copy sequence; don't sort numerically.
- Detect the repeated mask from aligned colored copies if multiple copies already exist; use only the motif's foreground cells, not its bounding-box zeros.
- Verify each observed motif cell maps to the same relative offset in every copy and that all available demo copies remain unchanged.
- Do not confuse palette/key height or location with the motif. The key is metadata; the motif copies occupy their own stack.
- Critical output formatting pitfall: every row must have exactly the original width. A first attempt on the accepted 18×15 test used the correct rule and cells but accidentally had one row of width 16 (an extra zero), making the ARC grid invalid. Validate exact row count and every row width before submission, then ensure cells are 0–9.

# Continual-ARC task-c4b91aa4: replicate a template across divider panels

Use when a grid is partitioned by complete straight divider lines (often color 6) into congruent rectangular panels, one panel contains a colored pattern, and the other panels are mostly a uniform blank/background (observed as 1). Copy the template panel's contents into each corresponding panel, preserving the divider lines.

## Validated behavior
- Demo: 5×9 input with a full vertical divider column of 3 at column 4. The 5×4 panel to the left was uniform 7 (blank), while the right 5×4 panel held a pattern. Output copied the right pattern into the left panel, preserving the divider. Pattern pixels were copied exactly, including its 7-valued cells; this is panel replication rather than recoloring.
- Fresh test: 11×13 input with full horizontal divider row 3 and full vertical divider column 6 (both color 6), forming four 3×6 panels with 3×6 content spans. The top-left panel contained a 3×6 template; remaining panels were blank 1s. Output tiled the exact 3×6 template into all four panels, preserving both divider lines. Accepted.

## Additional accepted fresh test
- A 17×11 grid had divider rows 5 and 11 and divider columns 3 and 7, all color 4, producing nine congruent 5×3 panels. The top-left panel contained a sparse pattern (7s and a 9) on background 1; the other eight panels were blank 1. The accepted output repeated the top-left panel's complete 5×3 contents into every panel, preserving all divider rows/columns. This confirms tiling across a 3×3 panel layout, not just a single split or a 2×2 layout.

## Additional accepted fresh test
- A 17×29 grid had divider row 8 and divider columns 9 and 19, all color 3, yielding six congruent 8×9 panels (3 columns × 2 rows). The top-left panel contained a sparse template on background 1, including a 7 at its top-left, another 7, and a 0; all remaining panels were blank 1s. The accepted output tiled the entire top-left 8×9 panel across all six positions, preserving the divider lines. This confirms a 3×2 panel layout and exact copying of all template cells.

## Additional accepted fresh test: one populated quadrant as source
- An 11×15 input had a complete horizontal divider row 5 and complete vertical divider column 7, both color 1, creating four 5×7 panels. The bottom-right panel was populated on background 5; the other three panels were entirely 5. The accepted output copied the bottom-right panel's complete 5×7 contents (including its 5 background cells) into all four panels and preserved both divider lines. The source pattern was copied without rotation/reflection: e.g. its first content row `5 2 5 5 4 5 4` appeared at the same within-panel row and columns in every quadrant. This confirms the populated source panel need not be top-left and that exact, position-preserving tiling applies to a 2×2 arrangement.

## Additional demo evidence: horizontal replication
- In a 13×9 demo, the top 6×9 region held a nonuniform pattern, row 6 was a full divider of 5, and the lower 6×9 region was uniform 8. The output preserved the upper region and divider, then copied the entire top pattern unchanged into the lower region. The template may therefore be an entire large panel containing varied colors, not just sparse marks; all cells and their within-panel positions matter.

## Procedure
1. Find complete divider rows/columns and treat them as immutable boundaries.
2. Identify congruent panel dimensions and locate the populated template panel.
3. Repeat the template panel's entire cell matrix into every other aligned panel, including template-colored/background cells; do not merely stamp non-background marks or recolor the blanks.

# Continual-ARC selective object recoloring

Use when a grid has a prominent colored guide (often an L-shaped line) and one or more other colored objects may be recolored to match it.

## Supported transformation model

Some instances preserve the grid except for exactly one selected non-background object/component, whose color becomes the guide color. This is an observed task family, not a universal ARC rule. First verify the transformation against every available demo: compare input and output cell by cell, identify the guide, mark every connected component, and account for all unchanged same-color objects. Preserve object shapes and holes if the demonstrated operation is a color substitution; do not extend the guide or move the object.

## Selector inference workflow

1. Identify background, guide color, guide geometry, and all other components. Use 4-connected components unless diagonal connectivity is demonstrated. Record component sizes, bounds, colors, shapes, and distances to the guide.
2. For each demo, list the exact changed component and the salient same-color / similar-shape components that were not changed. Distinguish facts from possible selector hypotheses.
3. Test candidate selectors across the full demo set: source color, component size, shape, location, relative orientation, distance, or combination. A candidate is not established merely because it fits one example; explain counterexamples and negative evidence.
4. Before paying for a demo, explicitly name at least two test-relevant competing hypotheses and how their predictions differ on the current test. Request another pair only when a plausible outcome can discriminate those predictions. Do not reflexively request all available demos just because the rule remains unclear.
5. If the selector remains ambiguous, do not choose a visually salient object without evidence. Use a demo if the expected information is worth its cost; otherwise submit only when one prediction is demonstrably better supported.
6. Construct the output by copying the input and recoloring only the selected component. Verify dimensions, unchanged guide/background, no unintended changes, and exact component boundaries before responding.

## Strict interaction format

In Continual-ARC turns, emit exactly one legal action JSON object on the final line; if the protocol requires strict JSON, provide no explanatory prose. Track demo and wrong-submission costs and caps. See `references/task-d5c34891-observations.md` for one six-demo recurrence where the recoloring operation was clear but the target selector was not.

## Pitfalls

- Do not recolor every component of a source color: demos may leave similar objects untouched.
- Nearest-to-guide, largest, smallest, singleton, and shape matching are hypotheses, not defaults.
- Do not call an unresolved selector “contextual” and then spend demos without identifying how their outcomes alter test candidates.
- Recolor the component, not its bounding box; preserve holes, background, and adjacent objects.

# Continual-ARC task-01713300 evidence

## Observed task form
Two demonstrations show a full uniform divider line separating panels. Output dimensions match the panel containing the randomized/sparse symbols, with divider and other panel removed. However the exact transformation of the selected panel is unresolved: output colors are 3/5, and the test's simple candidates all failed.

### Demo 1
Input 27x25. Full row 13 (zero-based) is all 7. Output is 13x25, precisely input rows 14–26; top 13 rows and divider dropped. Lower panel input uses 0 and 5. Output contains 3 and 5.

### Demo 2
Input 13x23. Full column 11 (zero-based) is all 0. Output is 13x11, corresponding to columns 0–10; columns 12–22 and divider removed. Output uses 3 and 5. Thus selected panel can be below or left; identify the randomized-pattern panel, not a fixed orientation.

## Test with unresolved rule
Test was 25x18. Full horizontal divider row 12 (color 1). Above: 12x18 mostly 2, with one 9 at (9,1). Below: 12x18 sparse 9s on 0. Eight submissions all failed, including invalid output once. Attempts included all-2 panels, lower panel with background 3 and original 9s replaced by 2, selected panel mapped to 5/3 based directly on 0/9 cells, and lower panel mapped to 2/3. These simple recoloring/preservation approaches are ruled out. No correct output known.

## Confirmed correspondence rule from an additional demo
A further demo input was 17x11, with a full horizontal row of 0 at zero-based row 8, separating two aligned 8x11 panels. The top panel used colors 9/8; the lower panel used 9/7. Output was 8x11 and exactly compares corresponding cells: output 3 when upper and lower cells are equal, otherwise 9. Examples: at (0,0), both are 9 → output 3; at (0,1), 8 vs 9 → output 9; at (0,3), 9 vs 9 → 3. This establishes a cellwise equality mask, with equal→3 and unequal→9, rather than direct extraction or recoloring of either panel. Divider is removed; output corresponds to the aligned panel dimensions. This new demo's palette differs from earlier demonstrations that used 3/5, so derive output palette from all current instance demos or their established mapping rather than blindly generalizing the old palette.

## Current 16x25 recurrence test and attempt audit
Input has a full vertical divider of 0 at column 12, leaving two aligned 16x12 panels (left columns 0–11, right columns 13–24). Compare left[r][c] with right[r][c+13]. The right panel is all 7 except one 5 at global coordinate (14,14); the corresponding left-panel cell is 5 at (14,1). Thus these panels differ everywhere except local coordinate (14,1). Applying the just-demonstrated equality rule with its palette gives a 16x12 output of 9 everywhere except output[14][1]=3.

Important attempt history: eight submissions were exhausted, all incorrect. Several repeatedly submitted the left panel cellwise transformed 4→3 and 5→9 (with the singleton right-side mark not incorporated), or a variant baseline 4/9. Two sparse guesses put 3 at (14,1), but incorrectly used baseline 4 or 9? Specifically the earliest all-4 grid with a 3 at (14,1) was incorrect, and later all-9-with-3-at-(14,1) also incorrect; the equality insight was recognized too late and the scoring feedback means the proposed equality output is not verified accepted for this instance. Other failed ideas included constant grids and simple selected-panel recoloring. Do not claim the inferred output was accepted: although the additional demo strongly supports equality comparison, the instance ended at the attempt cap with no successful submission. This discrepancy means a hidden detail/palette/orientation or transcription issue may remain; validate rule against every earlier demo before relying on it.

## Accepted recurrence confirmation: 8x27 test

A fresh 8x27 test had a full vertical divider of 7 at column 13, producing two aligned 8x13 panels. The left panel used 6 as its background with scattered 9s; the right panel was 8 throughout except for a single 6 at row 7, local column 11. The accepted output was 8x13: color 6 everywhere except color 3 at (7,11). The only corresponding equal pair was left 6/right 6 at (7,11); all other pairs differed. This confirms the cellwise comparison rule on a vertical split: equal→3, unequal→the first/left panel's background color (here 6). The exact output is `[[6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6],[6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6],[6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6],[6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6],[6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6],[6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6],[6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6],[6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,3,6]]`.

## Updated rule: aligned-panel comparison, shared-color default

For a full-line divider between aligned panels, compare corresponding cells. Output 3 where the two cells are equal; at unequal positions, output the unique color shared by the two panels' palettes (the intersection of their cell-value sets). Output shape is one panel's dimensions, with the divider excluded. This shared-color default is not necessarily the first/top/left panel's background; do not assume that without checking the panel palettes.

### Evidence across orientations and palettes

# Continual-ARC task-76e81bcb: decode 3×3 blocks

Partition the input grid into non-overlapping 3×3 blocks, scanning from the top-left. For each block, ignore all cells with color 5. Emit the unique remaining color as the corresponding output cell. If the block contains only 5s, emit 0. Output dimensions are input height/3 by input width/3.

- If both interior dimensions are odd, fill every interior cell with 7.
- If both interior dimensions are even, fill every interior cell with 2.

Observed examples are square frames, so the demonstrated parity classes coincide across height and width: interiors 1×1, 3×3, and 5×5 are filled with 7; interiors 2×2 and 4×4 are filled with 2. The test included several 3×3 hollow frames with varied outline colors; all centers became 7. Background and outline colors vary; do not assume outline color determines fill.

## Evidence

- Demo 1: a 3×3 color-4 frame on background 8 had its 1×1 interior changed to 7. A 6×6 color-9 frame and 4×4 color-0 frame had 4×4 and 2×2 interiors filled with 2.
- Demo 2: 3×3 frames (colors 3, 4, 5) were filled at center with 7; 5×5 frames (colors 9 and 8) and a 7×7 color-8 frame had odd-sided interiors filled with 7. A 6×6 color-8 frame had its 4×4 interior filled with 2.
- Fresh test: five 3×3 frames on background 3, with outline colors 1, 0, 6, and 5, had each center changed to 7; outlines and background otherwise remained unchanged. This was accepted.
- Fresh test: on a 21×29 background-6 grid, an 8-colored 4×4 frame had its 2×2 interior filled with 2, and a 5-colored 5×5 frame had its 3×3 interior filled with 7; all else was preserved. The submission was accepted.

## Application checks

1. Locate complete one-cell-thick rectangular outlines; measure the enclosed interior dimensions, excluding the perimeter.
2. Apply parity-based fill to interiors only, preserving the complete perimeter.
3. Preserve all non-frame cells and verify dimensions and row/column coordinates before submitting.
4. Before serialization, verify the output has exactly the input row count and every row has exactly the input column count; invalid ARC grid formatting incurs a wrong attempt even when the intended transformation is correct. Prefer copying the input and changing only the identified interior cells.

## Additional fresh evidence

- Fresh 12×14 test, accepted with zero wrong attempts: on background 1, three separate 3×3 hollow frames with outline colors 8, 5, and 3 each had their single interior cell changed to 7. All frame perimeters, unrelated cells, and dimensions were preserved. Confirms same rule in a grid containing multiple frames with varied outline colors and positions.

- Fresh 20×29 test, accepted with zero wrong attempts: on background 1, a color-5 4×4 frame enclosed a 2×2 interior and was filled with 2; a color-4 7×7 frame enclosed a 5×5 interior and was filled with 7; a separate color-5 3×3 frame enclosed a 1×1 interior and was filled with 7.
